The statement strikes a cautious-dovish balance: keeping rates unchanged and emphasizing “patience” with inflation near 2 percent and expectations little changed. In New Keynesian terms, when expectations are anchored and current inflation is close to target, the marginal benefit of additional tightening is low (Woodford, 2003; Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido). The noted moderation in business fixed investment is consistent with evidence that tighter financial conditions and internal funding constraints depress investment (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994), reinforcing the case for caution. Moreover, low unemployment alongside stable inflation aligns with Friedman and Phelps’ view of no long-run inflation–unemployment trade-off, so strong labor markets do not, by themselves, warrant preemptive hikes. Framing policy as flexible inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson) supports waiting amid “muted inflation pressures” and softer market-based inflation compensation. Net tone: slightly positive for risk assets but tempered by global risks and softer investment, so a bit less upbeat than a purely growth-focused read.
